'''''Blumea balsamifera''''' is a [[flowering plant]] belonging to the genus ''[[Blumea]]'' of the family [[Asteraceae]]. It is also known as '''Ngai camphor''' and '''sambong''' (also '''sembung''').

==Description==
In the Philippines, where it is most commonly known as '''sambong''', ''Blumea balsamifera'' is used in traditional [[herbal medicine]] for the [[common cold]] and as a [[diuretic]].<ref name="stuart" /><ref name="manila" /><ref name="plant" />  It is also used for infected wounds, [[respiratory tract infection|respiratory infections]], and stomach pains in [[Thailand|Thai]] and [[China|Chinese]] [[traditional medicine|folk medicine]].<ref name="pmid21500092">{{cite journal| author=Uthai Sakee, Sujira Maneerat| title= Antimicrobial activity of Blumea balsamifera (Lin.) DC. extracts and essential oil | journal=Natural Product Research | year= 2011 | volume= 25 | issue= 19 | pages= 1849–1856 | pmid=21500092 | doi= 10.1080/14786419.2010.485573| s2cid= 205836759 |display-authors=etal| url= https://zenodo.org/record/887549 }}</ref>

The genus ''Blumea'' is found in the tropical and sub-tropical zones of [[Asia]], especially the [[Indian subcontinent]] and Southeast Asia. ''Blumea balsamifera'' is one of its species that is used in [[Southeast Asia]].  A [[weed]], this plant is a [[ruderal species]] that often grows on disturbed land,<ref name="stuart">[http://www.stuartxchange.org/Sambong.html Sambong listing at Stuart X Change list of Medicinal plants].  Accessed December 25, 2009.</ref> and in [[grasslands]].<ref name="plant" /> It has been described physically as:
{{quote|Softly hairy, half woody, strongly aromatic shrub, 1-4 meters (m) high. Simple, alternate, broadly elongated leaves, 7-20 cm long, with toothed margin and appendaged or divided base. Loose yellow flower head scattered along much-branched leafy panicles. Two types of discoid flowers: peripheral ones tiny, more numerous, with tubular corolla; central flowers few, large with campanulate corolla. Anther cells tailed at base. Fruit (achene) dry, 1-seeded, 10-ribbed, hairy at top.|Sambong listing at Stuart X Change list of Medicinal plants <ref name="stuart" />}}

==Use in the Philippines==
{{More medical citations needed|section|reason=Most sources are at least a decade old and come from news coverage or tertiary sources; with any journal articles mentioned only providing in vitro insights||date=August 2025}}
In most of the Philippines, ''B. balsamifera'' is called ''sambong'' in the [[Tagalog language]], but in [[Visayas]] it is known as ''bukadkad'' or ''gabon'', and in [[Ilocos]] it is sometimes called ''subusob'', ''subsub'', or ''sobsob''.<ref name="stuart" /><ref name="plant">{{cite web |url=http://www.bpi.da.gov.ph/Publications/mp/html/s/sambong.htm |title=Sambong = |accessdate=2009-12-25 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090226194651/http://www.bpi.da.gov.ph/Publications/mp/html/s/sambong.htm |archivedate=2009-02-26 }} - [[Bureau of Plant Industry (Philippines)|Bureau of Plant Industry]] of the Department of Agriculture of the Republic of Philippines Official government website.  Accessed December 25, 2009.</ref><ref name="sambong">[http://www.philippineherbalmedicine.org/sambong.htm Philippine Herbal Medicine website].  Accessed December 25, 2009.</ref>  Its primary uses are as a [[diuretic]] (or "water pill") and to treat symptoms of the [[common cold]].<ref name="manila">Bernardo M. Villegas, "Business and Society: High-value crops", ''[[Manila Bulletin]]'', November 29, 2009, found at [http://www.mb.com.ph/articles/231732/highvalue-crops Manila Bulletin] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091222140025/http://www.mb.com.ph/articles/231732/highvalue-crops |date=December 22, 2009 }}.  Accessed December 25, 2009.</ref><ref name="plant" /><ref name="sambong" />  As a diuretic, sambong is an herb used to treat [[urolithiasis]] (urinary tract or [[kidney stone]]s) and [[urinary tract infection]]s,<ref name="manila" /> and thus reduces [[high blood pressure]].<ref name="sambong" />  Sambong works as an [[expectorant]], an [[anti-diarrheal|antidiarrheal]] and an [[antispasmodic]], all of which treat some [[symptom]]s of the common cold.<ref name="stuart" /><ref name="manila" /><ref name="plant" /><ref name="sambong" />  It is also sometimes used as an [[astringent]] for wounds.<ref name="stuart" /><ref name="sambong" />  It is approved by the Philippine Department of Health, Institute of Traditional and Alternative Health Care,<ref name="sambong" /> and by the Bureau of Plant Industries of the Department of Agriculture.<ref name="manila" />

''No'' claim has been made by any responsible practitioner that it would [[cure]] the common cold or [[kidney disease]], and it has "No Approved Therapeutic Claims". Rather the only legitimate claim is that it relieves symptoms.<ref name="manila" /><ref name="plant" />

The active ingredients exist in the [[volatile oil]], made from the leaves of the sambong, which have mostly [[camphor]] and [[limonene]], but also has traces of [[borneol]], [[saponin]], [[sesquiterpene]], and [[tannin]].<ref name="stuart" /><ref name="plant" />

Sambong is available as a tea, and may be purchased commercially.<ref name="manila" /><ref name="plant" />  The tea has a woody taste, with hint of [[menthol]], described on an official [[Government of the Philippines]] website as "a strong camphoraceous odor and a pungent taste".<ref name="plant" />

==Uses elsewhere in Asia==

In [[Thai folklore]], it is called Naat (หนาด) and is reputed to ward off spirits.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bangkokpicture.com/unusual/maenak.php|title=The Legend of Mae Nak Phra Khanong at Wat Mahabut, Bangkok, Thailand|publisher=Bangkok Picture|accessdate=29 January 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131226134230/http://www.bangkokpicture.com/unusual/maenak.php|archive-date=26 December 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref>  It is also used in the treatment of infection.<ref name="pmid21500092"/>

In addition, it is used in [[traditional Chinese medicine]],<ref name="pmid21500092"/> in [[Malays (ethnic group)|Malay]] folk medicine, and in [[India]]n [[Ayurvedic medicine]].<ref name="Bhuiyan">{{cite journal | author= Md. Nazrul Islam Bhuiyan, Jasim Uddin Chowdhury | title= Chemical components in volatile oil from Blumea balsamifera (L.) DC. | journal= Bangladesh Journal of Botany | year= 2009 | volume= 38 | issue= 1 | pages= 107–109 | url= http://www.dhakai.com/botany/journal-June%202009/articles/Art.%2017.pdf | display-authors= etal | access-date= 2010-03-01 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110709020121/http://www.dhakai.com/botany/journal-June%202009/articles/Art.%2017.pdf | archive-date= 2011-07-09 | url-status= dead }}</ref>

Besides its medicinal uses, it may also be used as a decorative dry plant. The [[Bodo–Kachari people|Bodos]], of [[Assam, India]], use it as a flavourful herb and add it to soups, chicken, curries, and also as a side dish with chillies and native soda ash water called ''[[khardwi]]''.{{citation needed|date=September 2022}}
